reading.body:
Defense AI procurement is documented in free federal databases, SAM.gov, USAspending, and FPDS, with the Defense Innovation Unit as the commercial entry point and subscription analysts layered on top.

The free sources are the primary record. SAM.gov lists solicitations and awards, USAspending carries every federal award, and FPDS records contract actions and vendor performance at the transaction level. DIU is where commercial AI enters DoD programs, with public project listings. Govini builds decision science on that record, and Silicon Valley Defense Group maps the commercial entrants.

The programs of record are decision support, autonomy, and ISR processing, the AI applications the sector tracks. Tracking them through procurement data shows actual spending and vendor capability, not just announcements. What the data does not show is compute demand, building capacity, or power requirements, none of those appear in these sources. Government AI labs are catalogued separately, not here.

summary: Decision support, autonomy, and ISR processing are the programs of record; DIU is the commercial on-ramp. Who tracks the sector: free government procurement databases are the primary record, with dedicated defense-intelligence firms layered on top - this page starts with the sources anyone can verify.

analysis.body:
The material available for defense does not include a measured adoption rate. No Census Bureau figure appears in this JSON, and no source here reports a percentage of defense organizations using AI, so any number would be invented. What the sources do show is where defense AI activity is recorded and who intermediates it. SAM.gov is described as the government's own system of record for federal contract opportunities, carrying AI-related Department of Defense solicitations, awards, and vendor registrations, free and searchable. FPDS is described as the underlying procurement system, recording DoD contract actions and vendor performance history at the transaction level, and USAspending is described as carrying every federal award, downloadable, built on the Federal Procurement Data System feed. For a reader trying to see what is actually being bought, these three are the primary evidence trail rather than any analyst summary.

On deployment, the curated points describe decision support, autonomy, and ISR processing as programs of record. That is the shape of defense AI use this page covers: intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance processing, autonomous systems, and tools that support command decisions, rather than general-purpose office automation. The Defense Innovation Unit is described as where commercial AI enters DoD programs, with public project listings, and its own page states its mission is to convert entrepreneurial products into tangible combat power. That makes DIU the commercial on-ramp for vendors without an existing prime relationship.

Where vendors and money concentrate is partly visible through the procurement record and partly through the analysts who interpret it. Govini is described as the defense-intelligence platform used inside the Department, tracking procurement trends, supply-chain risk, and vendor capability in AI and autonomy, and publishing public scorecards on critical-technology spending. Janes is described as a long-running defense analysis provider maintaining databases of contractors, programs, and procurement forecasts, a subscription source. Silicon Valley Defense Group is described as a nonprofit monitoring the intersection of commercial tech, private capital, and national security, publicly mapping the companies driving AI adoption in the DoD space. The curated points label the free federal procurement data first and the subscription analysts as named for completeness, which is a fair guide to which sources a reader can actually check.

The sources are largely silent on ROI. Nothing in this JSON reports cost savings, efficiency gains, or return figures from defense AI deployments, and no source states a percentage on that question. What can be said is structural: government AI labs are catalogued separately, and the page on them notes that state-funded labs carry public mandates and draw on sovereign budgets rather than venture capital or product revenue, which shapes what they build and why. The two entries there, Technology Innovation Institute in Abu Dhabi and Shanghai AI Laboratory in China, are described as able to command infrastructure commitments, including compute and facilities, that market-driven labs must negotiate for commercially. That is a statement about funding structure, not about returns.

On risk and regulatory posture, the material is thin and mostly procedural. SAM.gov notes that the system contains Controlled Unclassified Information and that viewing, reproducing, or disposing of it must follow 32 CFR Part 2002 and GSA Order CIO 2103.2 CUI Policy, and that the system is subject to monitoring. The same page records administrative changes, including revisions to ISR eligibility logic in the Subcontracting Plan Reporting system, the retirement of the FPDS.gov ezSearch feature with contract award searches moving to SAM.gov, and the retirement of the Electronic Subcontracting Reporting System as part of modernizing federal acquisition systems. Janes describes applying strict criteria for source credibility and peer review to produce decision-grade intelligence, and describes sharing unclassified intelligence across domains and partners to enable interoperability. Beyond that, the sources do not set out a defense-specific AI regulatory regime.

For a reader deciding whether to deploy, the practical takeaway from this material is about evidence rather than enthusiasm. The free record on SAM.gov, FPDS, and USAspending is where AI-related defense solicitations, awards, and vendor performance can be checked directly, and DIU is the named commercial entry point. Govini, Janes, and Silicon Valley Defense Group offer interpretation and mapping, but Janes is explicitly a subscription source. No source here supplies an adoption rate or an ROI figure for defense AI, so a deployment case will have to be built on the procurement record and on the reader's own pilot evidence, not on numbers this material provides.

https://www.svdg.org/.brief: The page presents Motiv, an agency run by Andrej Schindler and Jonas von der Gathen that describes itself as an "Agentur für Zukunftspotenziale", placing creative people with values-oriented companies. It says it connects people and companies, accompanies individual development and creates space for future perspectives, driven by curiosity about people and how organisations evolve. Companies are described as grown, unique organisms whose sense of purpose and urge to develop are their driving forces, and the agency says its aim is to place people who bring both professional expertise and the ability to connect with a company's purpose. It states that it works with companies holding social and ecological values and seeks long-term working relationships, and that it sees people as developing beings whose individual potential it tries to recognise at the right moment for a career step. The page also invites readers to register for a quarterly newsletter with open positions, accounts of company visits and interviews.

https://www.janes.com/.brief: Janes reports that it gathers information from vetted on-ground specialists, exclusive interviews, and events, acting as human sensors that web crawlers cannot reach. Janes reports that every data point is verified against reliable, vetted sources and that its dataset is the largest of its type, connecting millions of points to uncover patterns. Janes reports that its final content is peer reviewed to meet its quality and accuracy standards, and that it supplies validated data for the Joint Intelligence Preparation of the Operational Environment process. Janes reports that its digital portal lets users navigate validated data to uncover insights, moving from “what happened” to “what it means.”

https://www.govini.com/.brief: Govini says that Air is a leader in Enterprise Readiness and that its mission is to make readiness a real-time, continuously achieved condition. The company explains that its platform layer turns activated data into adaptive workflows, mobilized agents, and AI-driven orchestration that forecasts issues, prioritizes recommendations, and aligns resources.

https://theworldofai.org/ai-ecosystem/ec.brief: The page catalogues two government AI labs, each verified individually against a document the organisation published about itself, with the deciding source and its last-read date recorded. It states that Technology Innovation Institute in Abu Dhabi and Shanghai AI Laboratory in China share the government-lab classification but sit in very different political economies. TII is described as operating under Abu Dhabi's Advanced Technology Research Council and having published frontier open models, while Shanghai AI Laboratory is described as backed by national ministries and the Shanghai municipal government, placing it within China's central research priorities. The page argues that state-funded labs carry public mandates and draw on sovereign budgets rather than venture capital or product revenue, and that both can in principle command infrastructure commitments, including compute and facilities, that market-driven labs must negotiate for commercially.
